lead: Photoelectric sensors convert light into an electrical signal. A source sends a beam, and a receiver measures how much light arrives. If an object blocks, reflects or bends the beam, the receiver current changes and the sensor gives a switching or measurement output. Fibre optic sensors use the same idea but guide light inside a thin glass or plastic fibre, so the electronics can stay far from a harsh or live measurement point. You meet them in conveyor counting, safety guards, banknote scanners and strain or temperature monitoring on bridges.
prereq: You need: basic optics of reflection and refraction, and the idea of active and passive transducers.

sections.h3: Photoelectric effect and three beam arrangements

blocks.text: Photoelectric transducers use the photoelectric effect: light of frequency f delivers photons of energy E = hf. Here h is Planck's constant and f is frequency in hertz. If E is larger than the material's work function Φ, electrons escape and create current. Below the threshold frequency, brighter light gives no electrons. Above it, more light gives more current. That holds for photoemissive surfaces, where the threshold is the work function Φ. In a semiconductor receiver such as a photodiode the photon must instead exceed the band gap E<sub>g</sub> to free an electron-hole pair, so the longest usable wavelength is λ<sub>max</sub> = h c / E<sub>g</sub>. A photoelectric sensor therefore matches its light source to a receiver that responds to that wavelength.

Photoelectric transducers come in three classes. Photoemissive devices release electrons from a cathode into vacuum: the phototube and the photomultiplier tube. Photoconductive devices change resistance with light: the light-dependent resistor. Photovoltaic devices generate a voltage or current at a junction: the photovoltaic cell and the photodiode used without bias. See phototube and photomultiplier and photodiodes and cells for each device.
The beam can be arranged in three common ways. The table compares them.

sections.h3: Fibre structure, total internal reflection and numerical aperture

blocks.text: A fibre has a core of refractive index n<sub>1</sub> surrounded by cladding of refractive index n<sub>2</sub>, with n<sub>1</sub> > n<sub>2</sub>. Light entering the core hits the core-cladding boundary. If the angle inside the core, measured from the normal to the core-cladding boundary, is greater than the critical angle θ<sub>c</sub>, total internal reflection occurs and light stays in the core. The critical angle satisfies sin θ<sub>c</sub> = n<sub>2</sub>/n<sub>1</sub>.

blocks.where: NA is the numerical aperture, a dimensionless number; n<sub>1</sub> is the core refractive index; n<sub>2</sub> is the cladding refractive index.
θ<sub>a</sub> is the acceptance angle, the largest half-angle at the input for which light is guided; NA is the numerical aperture.

items: An LED launches light into the core.
The core guides light by total internal reflection.
A sensor head changes the guided light by bending, pressure or a shutter.
A photodiode converts the received light into current.

sections.h3: Fibre optic sensing, loss and applications

blocks.text: An intensity-modulated fibre sensor makes the sensor head change how much light reaches the photodiode. Bending, pressure or displacement moves a shutter or changes coupling, so received power changes. The receiver sees an absolute power, but the measurand is coded as the change from its rest value. Source drift can look like a measurement change, so a reference channel or ratiometric reading is used.

blocks.where: P<sub>in</sub> is input optical power in mW or W; P<sub>out</sub> is output optical power in the same unit; Loss(dB) is positive when P<sub>out</sub> < P<sub>in</sub>.

blocks.text: A fibre Bragg grating is a periodic change in the core refractive index. It reflects one wavelength. Strain or temperature shifts that wavelength, so the reading is encoded in wavelength rather than brightness.

items: Fibre sensors are immune to electrical noise because the signal is light.
They have no sparks at the measurement point and suit flammable areas.
They are small and can work over long distances.
Uses include counting, safety curtains, temperature and strain monitoring.

blocks.text: In medicine, a pulse oximeter clipped on a finger is a through-beam photoelectric sensor: red and infrared LEDs on one side, a photodiode on the other. Fibre-optic pressure sensors on catheter tips read blood and intracranial pressure, and fibre temperature probes work inside MRI scanners because they carry no metal and no current.

examples.question: A fibre optic link launches 1 mW and receives 0.2 mW after 2 km. Find the loss in dB and in dB/km.
steps: Input power P<sub>in</sub> = 1 mW; received power P<sub>out</sub> = 0.2 mW; length = 2 km.
Loss per km = 6.9897 dB / 2 km = 3.49485 dB/km ≈ 3.49 dB/km.
examples.answer: The loss is 6.99 dB, which is 3.49 dB/km over 2 km.
examples.check:
import math
p_in = 1.0
p_out = 0.2
length_km = 2.0
loss_db = 10 * math.log10(p_in / p_out)
loss_per_km = loss_db / length_km
print(round(loss_db, 2))
print(round(loss_per_km, 2))

examples.question: A fibre for a sensor has core index n<sub>1</sub> = 1.50 and cladding index n<sub>2</sub> = 1.45. Find (a) the critical angle at the core-cladding boundary, (b) the numerical aperture and (c) the acceptance angle in air.
steps: (a) sin θ<sub>c</sub> = n<sub>2</sub>/n<sub>1</sub> = 1.45/1.50 = 0.9667, so θ<sub>c</sub> = 75.2°, measured from the normal. A ray must meet the boundary at more than 75.2° from the normal, that is at less than 14.8° to the boundary itself, to stay in the core.
(c) θ<sub>a</sub> = sin⁻¹(0.384) = 22.6°. Light arriving within a cone of half-angle 22.6° about the axis is guided; steeper rays leak into the cladding.
examples.answer: θ<sub>c</sub> = 75.2°, NA = 0.384 and the acceptance half-angle is 22.6°.

traps: A fibre sensor reads a change in light. If the LED output drifts, the receiver sees a change that is not from the measurand. Use a reference channel or ratiometric measurement.
Through-beam, retroreflective and diffuse are not the same. Through-beam needs an emitter and a separate receiver; diffuse uses the object as the reflector.
Loss in dB is positive when P<sub>out</sub> < P<sub>in</sub>. Use 10 log₁₀ for optical power, not 20 log₁₀.
Numerical aperture is not the acceptance angle. NA is a number; the acceptance angle is sin⁻¹(NA) in degrees or radians.
The photoelectric effect has a threshold frequency. Increasing intensity below threshold does not start emission.

quiz.q: State the photoelectric effect in one sentence.
quiz.a: Light above a threshold frequency ejects electrons from a material, producing a current.

quiz.q: Name the three common photoelectric sensing arrangements.
Why does light stay inside the core of a fibre?
quiz.a: The core has a higher refractive index than the cladding. Light hitting the boundary above the critical angle undergoes total internal reflection.

quiz.q: A plastic-clad fibre has n<sub>1</sub> = 1.48 and n<sub>2</sub> = 1.46. Find NA and the acceptance angle.
A fibre optic strain sensor reading drifts when the LED current changes, although strain is constant. Explain the cause and one fix.
quiz.a: The sensor measures received light intensity, so LED output drift looks like strain. Use a reference channel or ratiometric measurement to cancel source drift.

quiz.q: Compare through-beam and diffuse sensors for a dusty conveyor.
quiz.a: Through-beam has a separate receiver and usually more margin, but dust on either window can block it. Diffuse uses the object as reflector and needs only one side, but dust and object colour change its range.

quiz.q: A link launches 0.5 mW and receives 0.1 mW over 1 km. Find loss in dB and dB/km.
quiz.a: Ratio = 0.5 / 0.1 = 5. Loss = 10 log₁₀(5) = 6.99 dB. Loss per km = 6.99 / 1 = 6.99 dB/km.

beyond: Not for the exam. Fibre Bragg gratings are written into the core with ultraviolet light and many can sit along one fibre, so a single cable reports strain at many points. Optical time-domain reflectometry times the backscattered light along a fibre to find loss and breaks; its phase-sensitive form, φ-OTDR, turns the fibre into a long microphone (distributed acoustic sensing). Search next for fibre Bragg grating, OTDR and distributed fibre sensing.
